summary: Defines extensions to OSPF and IS-IS to advertise the Traffic Engineering capabilities of routers, for example whether a router can act as a branch point for a point-to-multipoint LSP. Path selection for MPLS and GMPLS can then take those capabilities into account. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Routers shout out what special jobs they can do, so the planner picks routes only through ones that can actually do the job.

questions: how to advertise te node capabilities in ospf
what is the te node capability descriptor
ospf router information lsa te capabilities
ospf tlv type 5 te node capability
subtitle: How OSPF and IS-IS routers announce which traffic engineering jobs they can do, so paths avoid nodes that cannot do them.

tldr.problem: MPLS and GMPLS path computation knew about links but not about what each router could do, such as acting as a branch point of a point-to-multipoint LSP.
tldr.mechanism: A new TE Node Capability Descriptor, a set of bit flags, is carried in OSPF as a TLV in the Router Information LSA and in IS-IS as a sub-TLV in the Capability TLV.
tldr.outcome: Path selection can treat node capabilities as constraints, avoid nodes lacking a feature, or trigger a workaround for them. Routers that do not understand the new item ignore it.

facts.label: Expected change rate
facts.value: No more than once a day

today: RFC 5073 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Advertise Node Capabilities
sections.content:
MPLS traffic engineering already uses extensions to link state protocols (OSPF and IS-IS) to advertise TE link information for constraint-based routing. RFC 5073 adds the missing piece: TE node capabilities, which can be taken into account as constraints during path selection.

The RFC gives two kinds of examples. Data plane capabilities include being a branch LSR or a bud LSR of a Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Label Switched Path. Control plane capabilities include supporting GMPLS signaling for a packet LSR, or supporting P2MP TE LSP signaling. Knowing the latter lets a path avoid nodes that lack a feature, or trigger a mechanism to support such nodes, which helps backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: Planning a trip is easier if you know which stops have a restaurant and which do not. This lets routers tell the planner what each one can do.

sections.title: The TE Node Capability Descriptor
sections.content:
The descriptor is a variable-length set of bit flags. Each bit stands for one capability of a label switching router (LSR). It can be used in path computation to avoid nodes that do not support a TE feature in the control or data plane, or to trigger procedures to handle them, for example LSP hierarchy to support a legacy transit LSR on a P2MP LSP.

Five capabilities are defined:

  • B: the LSR can act as a branch node on a P2MP LSP.
  • E: the LSR can act as a bud LSR on a P2MP LSP, meaning it is both transit and egress.
  • M: the LSR supports MPLS-TE signaling.
  • G: the LSR supports GMPLS signaling.
  • P: the LSR supports P2MP MPLS-TE signaling.

The RFC notes that new capability bits may be added in the future if required.
sections.eli5: Think of five light switches, each labelled with a skill. A router flips on the switches for the skills it has.

sections.title: TLV Formats in OSPF and IS-IS
sections.content:
In OSPF the descriptor is a TLV of type 5. Its length is variable and a multiple of 4, and its value is an array of 32-bit words of flags, numbered from the most significant bit as bit zero. It follows the TLV format of the OSPF TE extensions: 2 octets for the type, 2 octets for the length, then the value.

In IS-IS it is a sub-TLV of type 1, with 1 octet for the type and 1 octet for the length. The value is an array of 8-bit units of flags, again numbered from the most significant bit as bit zero.

The bit assignments are the same in both: bits 0 to 4 are B, E, M, G and P. Bits 5 to 31 (OSPF) or 5 to 7 (IS-IS) are reserved for future assignment by IANA. Reserved bits MUST be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on reception. The bit field MAY be extended with extra 32-bit words (OSPF) or bytes (IS-IS), and unknown bits are treated as reserved.
sections.eli5: It is a row of on/off boxes. Boxes one to five already have names, and the rest are saved for later. If a box has no meaning to you, you leave it alone.

sections.title: Flooding and Update Rules
sections.content:
In OSPF the TLV is carried in a Router Information LSA (OSPFv2 Opaque type 4 and Opaque ID 0, or OSPFv3 function code 12). Because the information is used as a path selection constraint, its flooding scope is area-local: it MUST be in an OSPFv2 type 10 Router Information LSA, or an OSPFv3 one with the S1 bit set and the S2 bit cleared. In IS-IS the sub-TLV MUST be in a CAPABILITY TLV with the S flag cleared.

The item is OPTIONAL and MUST NOT appear more than once. In OSPF, if it appears more than once only the first occurrence is processed. A router MUST originate a new LSA (or IS-IS LSP) when the content changes, and otherwise follows the normal refresh rules.

If no descriptor is present, the node's TE capabilities are unknown. A change MAY trigger a CSPF computation but MUST NOT trigger a normal SPF computation. The capabilities are expected to be fairly static, changing through configuration or software upgrade, and not more than once a day.
sections.eli5: A router only tells its own neighborhood, not the whole world. It only updates the sign when something really changes, which is not often.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC says the new items do not introduce interoperability issues. An OSPF router that does not support the TLV silently ignores it, as specified in RFC 4970. An IS-IS router that does not support the sub-TLV silently ignores it, as specified in RFC 4971.

Absence has a meaning too: when the descriptor is missing, or when a word (OSPF) or octet (IS-IS) of flags is missing, those capabilities are unknown rather than absent.
sections.eli5: Routers that cannot read the sign simply walk past it. A missing sign means nobody knows, not that the answer is no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The descriptor is not used for SPF computation or normal routing, so it has no direct effect on IP routing. Tampering with it may, however, affect Traffic Engineering computation. The mechanisms that secure IS-IS Link State PDUs and OSPF LSAs, and their TLVs, can be used to secure this TLV as well.
sections.eli5: Someone who scribbled on the signs could confuse the route planner, so the usual locks that protect router messages should protect these too.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned value 5 for the OSPF TLV in the Router Information LSA TLV registry, and value 1 for the IS-IS sub-TLV in the CAPABILITY TLV sub-TLV registry. It also created one registry of capability bit flags shared by both protocols, as a sub-registry of a new base registry for IGP-TE registries that apply to both OSPF and IS-IS.

New bit numbers may be allocated only by an IETF Consensus action. Each bit is tracked by its number, the defining RFC and its name. Bits 0 to 4 were assigned to this document.
sections.eli5: A shared list keeps track of which box means what, so OSPF and IS-IS never disagree about it.

items.label: B
items.desc: Can act as a branch node on a P2MP LSP.

items.label: E
items.desc: Can act as a bud LSR on a P2MP LSP (transit and egress).
